Canadian Camping 



A Slight For Your Comp 

Nora Bailey 


Co-Director, Camp Macaza, P.Q . 

Educational Assistant. Mental Health Institute, Montreal. 


This is the season of the year when 
we are all busy garnering new ideas 
for camp. We go to conferences and 
we see the latest in camp equipment 
displayed; we listen to the newest ideas 
on programme planning, record keep¬ 
ing and staff training; we are able to 
discuss our particular problem' with 
experts. All winter we have been 
reading the camping magazines and 
making lists of new books to order. 
Some of us may have attended courses 
in order to help us to understand 
children better. All these things are 
important and useful in camping but 
to my mind, they are as the chaff the 
wind bloweth away if a*camp hasn’t a 
personality. I mean not only a per¬ 
sonality for the camp itself, but also a 
person or a group of persons in whom 
this personality is embodied—someone 
who is a living symbol of the ideals,' 
hopes and aspirations of the camp. If 
you think of the camps you have at¬ 
tended, or the camps you have visited, 
you will find that the values and the 
things that you took away from that 
camp are associated with a person or 
people. A camp needs more than a 
setting, equipment, psychology and 
efficiency, it needs a soul. And of all 
these things, the soul is the most im¬ 
portant. 

' Our children to-day are - becoming 
accustomed to the best that the mater¬ 
ial world an provide. Our schools, our 
health facilities, our playgrounds, etc., 
are constantly being rearranged and 
modified to provide the best equipment 


for children. But while we have been 
striving to provide the biggest and the 
best, it may be that our children are 
sometimes starving for contact with an 
ideal, an idea, a spirit. A camp can 
give this to children. ^Tong after they 
have forgotten if the camp had can^ 
vas covered docks, or electric light, or 
a professional theatre, they will carry 
in their hearts ideas, attitudes, stand¬ 
ards and feelings learned at camp. 
You can’t take the equipment home 
from camp but you can take the ideals! 
No camp will be remembered in the 
years to come for its physical set-up 
but, it will live in its influence in the 
minds and lives of children. 

If we talk to adults who were lucky 
enough to spend their childhood sum¬ 
mers in a good camp and we listen 
carefully to their recollections, they 
nearly always centre around a person. 
Some people are not able to express 
the idea clearly but we see in t their 
camp loyalties, their enthusiasm for 
camp friends of long ago, their interest 
in camping and the fact that they are 
sending their own children to camps, 
the strength of their camp experiences. 
This creative spirit in a camp has given 
to these adults something they can 
never forget, something they remember 
with warmth and affection years later. 
It is difficult to pin down'this intang¬ 
ible something. In one camp I know 
of, the leader can make simnle things 
into occasions for children, celebrations 
they will alwavs remember; in another 
it may be the leader’s imagination and 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1951 


7 



poetry that kindle the hearts of chil¬ 
dren; in another it may be that the 
leader always seemed to think you were 
a wonderful person, capable of any¬ 
thing; in another it may have been 
the leader’s ability to express the things 
of the spirit in a way that children 
could feel and remember. But in any 
case, they all had that intangible some¬ 
thing, they were all personalities, lights 
in their camps. 

We are familiar with the saying: “the 
best camps are built not on equipment, 


but on personalities”. I would make the 
last word “personality”. A camp needs 
a spirit—someone who can set the god 
high, who can guide us on the climL. 
who can inspire children and staff to 
be something better than they knoir. 
And with all our courses and books, I 
do not know of anything that offers 
a great deal in this quest for a camp 
personality. But I do know that ir 
encompasses the best that camping czzl 
offer to children in their efforts to 
grow into mature men and women. 


BOY IN THE WOODS 

Ne’er take a small boy through the woods 
Or you’ll be sold a bill of goods. 

Especially so 3 if you should hate 
To reach your favourite arm-chair late. 

He’ll find the darndest things to do. 

Alluring ventures to pursue. 

He’ll linger in a slimy bog 
To pester some poor, hapless frog. 

He’ll kneel beside a wayside pool, 

And with a stick just poke and fool. 

While short of threat to life and limb 
’Twill be a real task budging him. 

He’ll shinny up the tallest tree 
With faint thought of catastrophe. 

And little good to fuss and frown. 

He’ll take his own time coming down. 

He’ll wade through brush and brambles 
thick 

Wild berries sparse and small to pick. 

And by his skouts they might welt be 
A fitting feast for royally. 

He’ll have, perhaps, a moment calm 
When quietly he’ll trudge along. 

Then joyous shrieks a din will make 
f( Hey lookit. Dad! A snake—a snake!” 
And so, of course, he’s off again 
To chase the wriggly denizen . . . 

Ah yes, he’U feel the magic spell 
Which countless boys have known so well. 
While one thing • you. will surely learn 
Before your footsteps homeward turn : 

If you’d but let him have his way 
He’d in the wood forever stay. 

—Larry Hinde

Canadian Camping 



Canoe Trips That Pass 


C. H. Irwin, 


Director , Sherwood Forest Camp. 


In undertaking to write this critical 
article, I am fully aware that some may 
say “Why don’t you practice what you 
preach?” Perhaps it is because many of 
us are conscious of shortcomings that 
it is difficult to get camp people to 
write on practical subjects. Having, 
however, spent a good many years 
making my living travelling in the 
woods, I am particularly aware of 
canoe-trip problems. Our camp is 
situated at a veritable crossroads for 
water travel, therefore we see an aver¬ 
age cross-section of both boys’ and 
girls’ trips, including our own. We 
have a unique opportunity to observe, 
since at least sixteen camps travel these 
waters. 

That quite a number of camp direc¬ 
tors are not entirely satisfied with the 
operation of these voyages is evinced 
by comments and discussions, but it 
is not easy to correct some of the defi¬ 
ciencies. “If Youth but knew and 
Age could do”, is of course the root of 
the difficulty, but by no means all. 

We face the problem of trying to give 
large numbers of boys and girls a 
profitable, satisfying experience during 
a limited period at camp, with the 
available equipment and staff. These 
may be quite adequate under normal 
conditions, but if there are dozens of 
youngsters qualified and eager to take 
trips, and a prolonged spell of unsuit¬ 
able weather holds them back, there is 
bound to be pressure to get out as 
many trips as possible as soon as the 


weather clears, and possibly to send 
less experienced counselors in charge. 
Perhaps there is an urge also to make 
trips as quickly as possible so that wait¬ 
ing groups may use the equipment. 
During such periods all the more favor¬ 
able sites are likely to be occupied and 
camping trips arriving late in the day 
are forced to find less suitable sites. 
Some may, and do say, “Be hard- 
boiled. Let them go, regardless of 
weather!” In my opinion these people 
should not be in charge of campers. 
There are enough hazards at any time! 

Each season, of course, there are 
hundreds of trips where common sense 
rules and where everyone has a mem¬ 
orable and profitable time. Such trips 
are often the highlight of the whole 
camping experience. However, by con¬ 
trast, there is another side to the 
picture, and a knowledge of the mis¬ 
takes may lead to their correction. The 
camping movement may be hindered 
more by one poorly conducted trip 
which gets publicity than can be offset 
by the many which are well-conducted. 
We have only to think of a fiasco in 
the north in recent times, or a multiple 
fatality in our southern section many 
years ago which is still mentioned by 
parents almost every season. 

My first contact with camp canoe- 
trips was in 1921. Our timber recon¬ 
naissance party was camped on Manitou 
Lake on the north side of Algonquin 
Park at the end of the portage from 
Kiosk. It was pouring rain and blow- 


T or onto, Canada , April , 1951 


9 



ing and we were enjoying the shelter 
of our tents when we noticed a bedrag¬ 
gled procession going by. There were 
boys in their early teens, carrying as¬ 
sorted dripping pack sacks, duffle-bags 
and blanket rolls, and some older chaps 
carrying canoes on the trot. Curious 
to know what was behind this seeming 
height of folly, we enquired and learned 
that this was a canoe trip from a boys’ 
camp. They dumped their soaking 
duffle in to the canoes and away they 
went. A better preparation for trouble 
would have been hard to find, as one is 
more prone to take chances and be 
careless when one is uncomfortable and 
wet. 

The incidents which follow have 
come to my notice comparatively re¬ 
cently and within a few miles of our 
camp, and must be just a fraction of 
those which are ocurring in this one 
area and not differing greatly from 
those in other areas. A trip from a 
long-established camp crossed our lake 
at nine p.m. to look for a camping spot. 
The bovs were about twelve years of 
age. They had not eaten since noon 
and figured to make camp and pre¬ 
pare supper at that late hour. On a 
very windy evening last summer, a 
girls’ camp group came by in a very 
damp state, hours after they should 
have been camped for the night. While 
speaking of such lack of judgment, two 
cases might be mentioned of groups 
being swamped because those in charge 
failed to realize that in windy weather, 
although they left a calm shore, an off¬ 
shore breeze was piling up the waves 
on the opposite side. Tt is difficult to 
impress this simple fact on young 
people. 

Where did the idea originate that “it 
is sissy to take a tent on a canoe-trip”? 
The writer is proud to be a sissy in this 
respect, and would prefer to reduce 
bedding if necessary. After all, if not 


used, a tent can be spread under one for 
more protection while sleeping. Dur¬ 
ing a cool all-day or all-night down¬ 
pour, it is most unsatisfactory to have 
a group of youngsters trying to hide 
under canoes or groundsheets like a 
flock of young partridge-chicks hiding 
under leaves. It is much more prefer¬ 
able to listen to the patter of rain in 
the tent. Perhaps it is the lack of pro¬ 
per shelter which prompts many groups 
to travel in bad weather, on the as¬ 
sumption that they couldn’t get wetter 
anyway. Part of the opposition to 
tents may be due to the fact that old, 
heavy, leaky tents are good enough for 
trips, or it may be lack of skill in setting 
them up quickly. 

How best to arrange for a satisfactory 
night’s rest requires time and thought 
and cannot be done on a rush trip. Bal¬ 
sam boughs are fine if the balsam is 
handy, if one is allowed to use them 
and if the counselor knows how, and 
has time. This combination does not 
always exist, and a directress of a camp 
mentioned recently that the girls re¬ 
turned “tired out”. Naturally a trip 
is strenuous, but with better opportun¬ 
ity for rest, fatigue can be reduced. 
Privately owned cabins or shelters at 
convenient intervals, with built-in 
bunks, is a solution which some camps 
have found. 

Last summer a canoe was spotted in 
difficulty in the middle of the lake, 
unable to make headway against the 
wind. In the canoe were three young 
girls belonging to a canoe-trip. The 
canoes had become separated and those 
in charge had gone on into the next 
lake, while this canoe following did 
not know where to find the passage. 
The leader of the trip should insist that 
all canoes keep within easy hailing dis¬ 
tance. Always there is the urge to 
race for the next portage and t^> feel 
superior if the first to arrive. Thus, 


10 


Canadian Camping 


often canoes are out of range before 
the leader realizes it. That at least 
one of the counselors should be with the 
group at all times should not be neces¬ 
sary to emphasize, yet cases have come 
to our attention where, counselors have 
left their charges and gone off to a 
village, supposedly for supplies, but 
actually for entertainment. 

In these days everyone should be 
conscious of fire hazards, and yet in 
recent seasons, two good camp spots 
have been burned by careless canoe- 
trippers and we have found several fires 
burning after trips have pulled out, one 
of them on our own property. The 
matter too, of garbage disposal and 
toilet arrangements at camp-sites and 
along portages is becoming a source of 
annoyance. 

As a final illustration—a canoe-trip 
in charge of a man of mature years 
camped on a large island in Hawk 
Lake. The campers went for an ex¬ 


ploration tour with the leader. On the 
opposite side of the island from the 
canoes, a boy cut his knee on a rock. 
Two friends of mine building a cottage 
on the shore a third of a mile away 
heard some calls but thought nothing 
of it until a sudden scream, a hundred 
yards off-shore sent them running to 
their boat. They managed to pull out 
of the water an exhausted boy who had 
been allowed to swim to them for help, 
with his clothes on. He had rolled up 
his trousers but they kept slipping 
down and hampering him. The man in 
charge of this trip showed inexcusable 
indiscretion. 

As a group of camp leaders it is 
providential that we have been so for¬ 
tunate in avoiding more serious camp¬ 
ing trip accidents. Let us, however, 
make sure that mistakes of the past 
will be avoided in the future. Let us 
play our part better! 



A Good Camper. 

—does his share of the work. 

—is careful with fire. 

—maintains and leaves a clean camp. 

—observes rules governing the area used. 

—is friendly, cheerful , and helpful. 

—Fay Welch 
from (( When You Are In the Woods”. 


Toronto , Canada , April, 1951 


11 









HEAVE HO! 


Joyce Bertram, 
Camp Ouareau, P.Q. 


The young camper walking gingerly 
along the beach in her bare feet, will, 
quite obviously, be late for dinner. Her 
once clean shorts are soaking wet and no 
longer clean. Her T-shirt, (also soak¬ 
ing wet) is plastered tightly across her 
shoulders. Her hair is lank and wind¬ 
blown. Her arms ache from the finger 
tips up, and her brain is reeling with 
all the new facts recently assimilated. 
But on her face is a beam you could 
spot at a distance of two city blocks, 
and in her eyes is the sparkle of a 
youngster who has just had the biggest 
thrill of her life. She has spent the 
morning sailing! 

The sailors in any camp are apt to 
be found walking gingerly along in 
bare feet. Nine times out of ten their 
shorts and T-shirts are soaking wet. 
Quite often their hair looks as if it 
hadn’t had a nodding acquaintance 
with a comb since the day camp open¬ 
ed. But ALWAYS they will be found 
with a large beam and sparkling eyes. 

If you spot two or three campers 
squatted down Indian-style in the 
middle of the path, chances are they 
are figuring out wind directions on a 
homemade compass hastily scrawled 
in the dust. If you see two or three 
more youngsters at the dinner table 
madly pushing forks and spoons around 
glasses and salt cellars, they’re not just 
making a nuisance of themselves or 
just idly filling in time, they’re prob- 
ablv trying to figure out a couple of 
tricky rules of Right of Way. 

For sailing is not a sport about which 


people are luke-warm. Reactions to 
the very word “sailboat” usually take 
but two forms, either a polite indiffer¬ 
ence or a mad enthusiasm. There 
seems to be no middle course. 

This mad enthusiasm, with which 
most campers become infected, will 
often express itself in a perfect willing¬ 
ness to spend a windless day down at 
the sailing dock, working their heads 
off cleaning boats, varnishing rudders 
and tillers, mending sails, splicing 
ropes, or even taking the entire sail 
off and re-bending it. There are a 
dozen jobs around the boats which can 
be reserved for the inevitable days 
when the wind refuses to materialize. 
Then the true sailor can echo the sen¬ 
timents of Ratty in “Wind in The Wil¬ 
lows” that “there is nothing in the 
world like just messing about with 
boats . . . just messing about.” 

To interest youngsters in sailing is 
easy; to keep their interest throughout 
the learning period, is sometimes slight¬ 
ly more difficult. Children who are 
eager to sail are eager to sail and “land 
sailing” should be cut to the minimum 
if there is a breeze large enough to dig¬ 
nify by the name. There are about ten 
parts of a small boat which should be 
learned immediately; things like boom, 
gaff, tiller, rudder, centreboard, trav¬ 
elling bar, sheet, halyards, belaying 
oins, stays, etc., but other parts mav be 
learned as the need for them arises. 
And incidentally, it is a good idea to 
use nautical terms wherever possible, 
so that youngsters get used to them 
right away. Some, like cast-off, make 


12 


Canadian Camping 



fast, come about, heave to, are almost 
self-explanatory and should come 
easily to their lips after a lesson or two. 

When the boat starts to heel, many 
people immediately are terrified, feel¬ 
ing that a watery grave is but a matter 
of moments away. It is of paramount 
importance therefore that the person 
in charge explain that sailboats are so 
designed as to sail better when they 
are “on their side’ 5 . Indeed, almost the 
best position for a boat, when running 
close-hauled, is with the water to the 
gunwhale of the leeward deck. It is 
unwise to suppose, however, that the 
farther the boat heels, the faster it will 
go. A deck can drag in the water and 
slow your progress just as effectively 
as an anchor. 

Almost the first question a camper 
asks when you tell them to pull in the 
sail or let it out, is “why?” When it 
looks all right the way it is, why change 
it? If a camper never remembers an¬ 
other thing you say, all is not lost if he 
or she can be made to realize that the 
set of the sail is all-important. And 
the correct set of the sail is JUST THIS 
SIDE OF THE LUFF. To be sure 
your sail is correctly set, let it out until 
it luffs, then pull it in just enough to 
stop the luff. To haul it in past this 
point, may increase the angle of your 
boat, but it won’t increase the speed. 
And sometimes, in that connection, I 
think it would be wise for each camp 
to paste a notice up near the foredeck 
where the skipper could not help but 
see it. “WHEN YOU GO DOWN 
WIND, LET YOUR SAIL OUT!” 
To my mind, there is no more unnerv¬ 
ing experience than to see a boat trav¬ 
elling downwind with its sail close- 
hauled. Not only is it very poor sail¬ 
ing, but may easily lead to an acciden¬ 
tal jibe, than which there is nothing 
more disorganized. 


“Jibe” is almost the first word in a 
would-be sailor’s vocabulary. And its 
connotation is usually rather fearsome, 
conjuring up as it does vivid pictures 
of an upturned boat and a skipper 
floating face-down in the water with 
a split in the side of his head. But, 
when the wind is steady, there is no 
excuse of an accidental jibe. 

There are places when a jibe is ex¬ 
pedient and even necessary and its 
correct use should be taught from the 
first. There is a special technique 
which should never vary, no matter 
how light the wind. In most cases, 
the sail is out rather far before a jibe. 
It should be hauled in quickly while 
the boat’s bow is headed away from 
the wind. When the wind catches the 
sail on the other side, the sheet should 
be allowed to run through the hands 
quickly so that there will be no resis¬ 
tance against it. The tiller, mean¬ 
while, is rapidly centred once more. In 
the case of an accidental jibe, the wind 
catches the sail and promptly lifts it up 
prior to sending it crashing to the other 
side. At first sign, therefore, of the 
boom starting to rise 5< push the tiller 
tov/ard it and send the boat upwind 
once more. Accidental jibes are* caused 
by a sudden change in wind direction, 
a sail which is not out far enough, too 
much weight on the windward deck, 
or a sudden movement on the part of 
crew which sets the boat rocking. 

When the youngsters become pro¬ 
ficient at handling the sheet and tiller, 
there are many techniques which may 
be employed which will improve their 
skill. Racing is one of the best teach¬ 
ers, for it takes a real skipper to bring 
one boat in ahead of the other when 
both boats are identical. The way it 
is done, of course, is by speed and ac¬ 
curacy in hitting the starting line, speed 
in coming about or jibing, proper dis- 


T or onto, Canada , April, 1951 


13 



tribution of weight and correct use of 
the rules of Right of Way. These rules 
may seem dull when they must be 
memorized. When they mean the 
difference between making a buoy on 
the second tack and not making it until 
the third, they assume first importance. 

There are many types of races be¬ 
sides one for straight speed. One 
which we have found popular at our 
camp calls for a bit of preparation 
first, but it is worth it. If there are 
three boats competing, take 18 or 24 
shingles or light pieces of wood and 
paint them white. On these shingles, 
paint an equal number of 1, 2 and 3. 
Then, before the start of the race, take 
these shingles about a quarter of a 
mile upwind and toss them into the 
water. The object of the race is to 
sail out and pick up as many of your 
own number as you can find. If you 
should be so unfortunate as to pick up 
a 3 when your own number is 2, you 
place the shingle back in the water 
FACE DOWN naturally, to make it 
harder for your opponents. This kind 
of racing calls for rapid handling of the 
boat and an accurate knowledge of 
rules of Right of Way. If there is a 
good wind this can be very exciting, as 
there is always the danger of the 
shingles drifting into shore before they 
can be spotted by a sharp-eyed mem¬ 
ber of the crew. 

A race from the dock is fun too. 
Crews must wait for the signal before 
running for their boats, and then they 
must rig the boat neatly and cast-off. 
This takes practice and provides a lot 
of fun for spectators too. 

Or try having the crews paddle their 
boat to a starting point and then put 
up their sails in the middle of the 
lake. Have them finish their course 
using a paddV for a rudder. Jt is some¬ 
times a good idea for young skippers to 


have this experience close to the home 
port, should the horrifying time ever 
come when the rudder snaps or decides 
to float away. 

If all directors were to see the broad 
grins on the faces of competent young 
people who handle their little boats as 
if they had been built into them, who 
race them against the elements and 
bring them back to the starting line in 
shipshape condition, who spend happy 
hours bailing and washing and shining 
up a favourite boat, or laboriously sew¬ 
ing numbers on a sail before a big race, 
they would think twice before saying 
they were too expensive. 

And if they, too, could experience 
that out-of-.this-world feeling which 
comes to a sailor on his first solo trip, 
when the boat under his hand responds 
to his every whim, when the wind and 
weather are elements to be battled and 
tamed, when the white sail and the 
blue sky and the scudding clouds and 
the flying spray are the only realities 
in a troubled world, then there would 
be a fleet of sailboats in every camp.

Canadian Camping 



So. You Think Your Covered 

M. H. Crone, 

Maryland Casualty Company, 

Canadian Managers—Robert Hampson and Son Limited, Montreal and Toronto. 


In the last issue, we wrote an article 
under the same caption, but confined 
our remarks to Fire Insurance. In this 
article we shall try, in the small space 
allotted, to convey to you some 
thoughts on Liability Insurance. 

Most of you will be quite familiar 
with Liability Insurance as applied to 
the operation of your automobile. The 
large majority of people and corpora¬ 
tions carry automobile Liability Insur¬ 
ance because they know that a negli¬ 
gent act in the operation of a motor 
vehicle may result in their being named 
as a defendant in a law suit which 
could have catastrophic results to their 
bank accounts, their property and 
their means of livelihood. What many 
people do not realize, however, is the 
fact that either the ownership or the 
operation of a business places on them, 
through Common Law, the responsi¬ 
bility of the safety of the public whom 
they are serving and the safety of their 
property. While Provincial Govern¬ 
ments have introduced special legisla¬ 
tion regarding automobile insurance, it 
is British Common Law throughout 
which governs the need for Bodily 
Injury and Property Damage Insur¬ 
ance which you need to protect you 
against loss through claims arising from 
.the operation of your automobile, your 
business and your personal pursuits. 

Let us now assume that you agree 
that Liability Insufance is a necessity 
for the operation of your Camp and 
that you have already consulted your 


Insurance Agent and purchased a 
Policy to give you that “protected” 
feeling. Feels good, doesn’t it! Well, 
don’t pat yourself on the back until you 
have considered the following points: 

(a) Policy Limits. Many businessmen 
today, still carry insurance with the 
old standard limits of $5,000.00 
for death or injury to one person, 
$10,000.00 for death or injury to 
to two or more persons in one 
accident and $1,000.00 for dam¬ 
age or destrution of property be¬ 
longing to others. If you read 
your newspaper you cannot help 
notice the facts that injuries or 
death to people, due to negligent 
acts, results in law suits for sums 
which stagger the imagination. A 
recent case resulted in a judgment 
of $115,000 to a man who was 
permanently disabled who had an 
earning capacity of $14,000.00 per 
year. Would your present insur¬ 
ance protect you against loss from 
a similar occurrence? Is there 
any guarantee you will never be 
faced with the problem of several 
guests being burnt to death or 
drowned through a negligent act 
of one of your employees? Think 
it over and check your policy 
limits. Inadequate insurance cov¬ 
erage can be as disastrous as no 
coverage at all. 

(b) A few camps operate aircraft, but 
most camps own canoes, rowboats, 

(Continued on page 27)

Behold Our New Crest! 


‘The die is cast’. The result which 
you see on this page is rather hand¬ 
some, don’t you think? 

Mr. D. P. Bromley of Toronto did 
the original drawings for CCA through 
Art Buckley and the Public Relations 
Committee. 

The Crest will not only appear on 
the new letterhead, but also on the new

CANADIAN CAMPERS’ CLUB 

A Canadian Campers’ Club! This 
idea took shape while talking with a 
group of campers about the Canadian 
Camping Association: They knew, 
of course, that Counselors had to be 
trained people, and that there could 
not be camps without counselors. And 
they had heard how this Association, 
as far as it was able, did all it could 
to help inspire and train young people 
to be real leaders. This group of 
youngsters had also been told of how 
boys and girls, right across Canada, 
rich and poor, with white skins and 
dark skins, sick children and crippled 
children, as well as healthy ones, went 
to camps, and all of them were learning 
things; and doing things, that people 
who did not go to' camp might not 
learn or do. They were told, too, of 
camps in South America, in England, 
and Holland, and some other parts of 
Europe. ‘It would be a grand idea, 
they thought, if we could have a Ca¬ 


nadian Campers 5 Club to which every¬ 
one who had gone to camp could be¬ 
long. Perhaps they could have a pin 
as have the Junior Red Cross, -the Bird 
Society—and even the Rotary, Lions 
and Kiwanis Clubs! It must not cost 
much—so just about every camper 
could afford one. Then there would be 
thousands of campers across Canada 
who would know, when they saw the 
pin, that the person who wore it had 
interests like themselves, and they 
would talk with each other about 
camping. Apd more people would 
want to help make it possible for more 
children to go to camp and enjoly our 
wonderful Canadian hills and forests, 
and lakes 5 . 

The C.C.A. thought it was a good 
idea too. We now want to launch this 
project in our Camps this summer. We 
have procured celluloid pins with a 
very attractive design, which the 
campers may Buy at a price of twenty- 
five cents (25c), at their respective 
camps. Incidentally, and this is a big 
factor in your promoting the idea — 
the C.C.A. would benefit financially by 
the sale of these pins. Order your sup¬ 
plies early in May, from the C.C.A. 
Office, 771 Burnside Street, Montreal, 
Que. Your order must be accompan¬ 
ied by a cheque, or money order. We 
believe the pins will “go like the pro¬ 
verbial hot cakes 55 

Do give us your interest and support. 
Let the youngsters feel that they are 
helping, by their interest, to make good 
camping possible for many other boys 
and girls.

ONTARIO 

The Ontario Camping Association 
has recently moved into a new and 
more spacious office at 52 Avenue Rd., 
Toronto (same telephone number, KI. 
0151). 

The Annual Conference is over and 
though registrations were sadly deplet¬ 
ed by the flu, it was nevertheless a most 
successful gathering with excellent 
addresses, discussion groups and fine 
commercial exhibits. The busiest de¬ 
partment at present is the Counselor 
Placement Bureau. So great is the in¬ 
terest here that camp directors and 
prospective counselors are urged to 
phone first for appointments. Plans 
are well advanced for the Counselor 
Training Course which will be held 
again this Spring commencing April 
18th. For five consecutive Wednesday 
evenings, the course will be given at 
Brown School, Avenue Rd. and on the 
last three Wednesdays there will be 
special sessions added for experienced 
counselors and department heads. 

QUEBEC 

With the National-Quebec Confer¬ 
ence only a few days away, the com¬ 
mittee in charge is busilv engaged in 
making the final preparations for the 
event. 

Ross Seaman, who is in charge of 
registration, has announced that regis¬ 
trations are pouring in thick and fast, 
and has given the following last minute 
instructions for those who have not yet 
registered: There is still time to register 
by mail. Just tear off the form on 
the folder you received in the mail and 
return it to the Quebec Camping As¬ 
sociation immediately. 

The conference will be held at Sir 
Arthur Currie Gymnasium, 475 Pine 
Avenue West. The exhibitors will have 
’their booths decorated in their usual 
colorful way. and soft music will be 
provided during the meals and between 
meetings. 

In sponsoring this conference, along 
with the Canadian Camping Associa¬ 


tion, the Quebec Camping Association 
hopes to establish a precedent whereby 
every two years a different province 
will be host to the rest of Canada at 
a National Camping Conference. 

SAM FREEDMAN, 
Conference Chairman. 

QUEBEC NOTES 

Most of the energies of the Quebec 
Association during the last month have 
been directed towards organizing the 
forthcoming conference. 

The Quebec members have greatly 
enjoyed the monthly programmes ar¬ 
ranged by our efficient programme 
chairman, Winona Wood. In Febru¬ 
ary, the meeting was devoted to Arts 
and Crafts, and those attending the 
workshop had a wonderful time making 
clay pottery, bamboo flutes, and 
whittling. In March a panel discus¬ 
sion was held on the subject of “Decen¬ 
tralized Camp Administration”. Miss 
Wood has announced that the Annual 
Meeting of the Quebec Association will 
take place on May 17, at the \MCA 
in the form of a supper meeting. 

Gem’al Ross Seaman, secretary of 
the QCA for the past two years, has 
been forced to resign from that position 
due to his recent appointment to the 
Lachine YMCA. Mrs. H. (Morgie) 
Morgenstern has been elected to re¬ 
place ffim for the balance of the year. 

Ruby Smith and Lauri Hutchison 
are hard at work re-organizing the 
Quebec membership system, and real 
results are expected from this commit¬ 
tee in the near future.

Booh Reviews 

BASIC SWIMMING: by Robert 
Kiphuth and Harry M. Burke; pub¬ 
lished, 1950, by the Ryerson Press, 
Toronto; pp 125; price, $3.75. 

The first part of the book clearly de¬ 
scribes and illustrates the “progres¬ 
sion” methods of teaching the basic 
strokes—crawl, side and breast—to be¬ 
ginners, be they children or adults. It 
also gives useful suggestioins for help¬ 
ing the beginner overcome fear of the 
water. The illustrations show the cor¬ 
rect positions in each progression of the 
stroke, both in and out of the water. 

The second part describes and illus¬ 
trates strokes and turns of competitive 
swimming. * These, too, are just as 
clearly explained as the basic strokes, 
with the usual effective illustrations. 

Swimming is excellent recreation for 
all. If one can swim with ease and 
confidence, it is much more enjoyable. 
“Basic Swimming” can assist the in¬ 
structor to help his or her pupils 
acquire or improve their swimming 
skills with ease and confidence. A 
splendid book for your swimming staff 
at camp! 

ABITIBI ADVENTURE: by Jack 
Hambleton; Longmans. Green & Co., 
Toronto 1; 1950; 173 pp.; price, 
$2.75. 

A good book for a camp library, par¬ 
ticularly in a boys’ camp. A story of 
the north country and its pulpwood op¬ 
erations, as the logs are cut, moved to 
the waterways and floated down in 
giant booms to the mill. The most 
exciting episode is a log jam which, in 
a few hours, piled thousands of cords 
of logs in a canyon-like passage of the 
Abitibi. Practically the whole popula¬ 
tion of Iroquois Falls (eleven miles 
down the river) turned out to watch 
the break-up, as a pilot maneuvred 


about, dropping his load of dynamite 
in strategic places over the jam. Down 
the canyon roared an ear-splitting re¬ 
verberation. *A foaming white wall of 
water, and logs tossed like matchwood, 
plunged into the swift-moving current 
and were soon in the raging rapids far 
below the jam. 

YOUNG BUSH PILOT: by Jack 
Hambleton; Longmans, Green & Co., 
Toronto 1; second edition, June, 
1950; 200 pp.; price $2.75. 

Another book by the same author as 
“Abitibi Adventure”, which would de¬ 
light boy-readers especially. The story 
relates the adventures of young Bill 
Hanson, bush pilot, who has thrilling 
experiences in helping to fight an epic 
forest fire in Ontario’s north country 
and in helping to track down a 
notorious poacher.,On all his journeys, 
Bill is accompanied by his faithful 
friend, an Irish Terrier, by the name of 
Mickey. 


WHEN YOU ARE IN THE WOODS: 

by Fay Welch. 

“No greater authority, or better in¬ 
terpreter of forest recreation can be 
found than Fay Welsh,” says the Dean 
of New York State College of Forestry, 
Toseph S. Illick. Those of us who 
heard his address on “Camping’s 
Unique Opportunity” at the recent 
Ontario Camp Conference felt that 
Fay Welsh was indeed an authority on 
the fundamentals of good camping. 
His little book “When You Are In the 
Woods” is full of helpful observations 
and tested conclusions. It is published 
by the New York College of Forestry 
as a public service and single copies 
may be obtained free. Price of copies 
in quantity quoted on request. Write 
to the Department of Public Educa¬ 
tion, Syracuse University, Syracuse 10, 
N.Y.

THE GAMP DIRECTOR’S HAND¬ 
BOOK AND BUYING GUIDE. 
1951 edition, official publication of 
American Camping Association, com¬ 
piled and edited by Galloway Pub¬ 
lishing Co., 705 Park Avenue, Plain- 
field, N.J. 140 pages, $1.00 in U.S., 
$1.50 elsewhere. 

This is the Fourth Annual Edition of 
the Handbook published by the editors 
of Camping Magazine. Changes have 
been made in editorial content, based 
on experience of camping people in 
using previous editions, and much new 
material has been added. • Among new 
material included is a 16-page Camp 
Director’s Callendar giving suggestions 
on what to do each month of the year, 
a compilation of selected motion pic¬ 
tures for camp use, a detailed chart on 
how to buy insurance, and many other 
similarly useful features. The new “lib¬ 
rary size” format, designed to make 
it easy for readers to keep the book on 
their shelves for ready reference, is 
again this year one of the “plus” fea¬ 
tures of the book. 

The Handbook is referred to by 
camping leaders as “a veritable gold 
mine of information for all people 
interested in or connected with camp 
operation.” It contains a vast amount of 
specific information needed in the suc¬ 
cessful operation of camps—charts, 
tables, diagrams and photographs. 
Sections of the book are devoted to 
food and food preparation, camp health 
practices, fire prevention methods, 
buildings and equipment, waterfront 
activities, campcraft and nature lore, 
arts and crafts, sports and games, di¬ 
mensions of playing fields and courts, 
and many other pertinent subjects. 
Another section contains a comprehen¬ 
sive list and descriptions of books on 
all phases of camp operation.

A RECOMMENDED 
HANDICRAFT FILM 

A film which we screened with much 
interest for incorporation in our craft 
and recreation programmes, was “Ani- 
mules”. This film produced and di¬ 
rected by Louis A. Shore, was given a 
Special Citation at the Canadian Film 
Awards, 1950. That the objective, to 
create a handicraft film which would 
invite participation from its audience, 
was achieved^ may be inferred from the 
statements of the award judges— 
“shows great imagination ... a unique 
teaching tool.” Our screening audi¬ 
ence felt that it was as successful in 
its utilitarian purpose of showing chil¬ 
dren how to make fantastic animals 
from common everyday materials, 
newspaper, wire, paste, as it was 
charming in its appeal to adults. An 
interesting feature of this ten minute 
sound and colour film was that it was 
the first educational film in which the 
complete commentary was spoken by 
one of the participating children. 

The film had its premiere at the 
Museum of Modern Art, New York,

GARBAGE DISPOSAL PIT 

For a safe, easy, fly-proof, odour- 
proof means of garbage-disposal at 
camp, dig a pit about 4 feet square. 
When you get down about 3 feet be¬ 
gin enlarging the pit to about 8 feet 
in diamteter, and continue to a depth 
of about 7 feet. * 

Choose sandy soil, if at all possible. 
If not available, gravel .and earth are 
also excellent. Clay is too difficult to 
dig, and is not suitable for proper seep¬ 
age. Be sure that the pit is at least 
150 feet from the lake and supply of 
drinking water. 

Using new 2” x 4” dressed lumber, 
construct two identical frames, like 
' picture frames, about two feet square. 
These frames are to be hinged together, 
‘like a box, and must be carefully con¬ 
structed so that when one is resting 
on the other (.with the 2”. faces touch¬ 
ing) they will fit exactly and tightly, 
and flies and ants will be unable to 
enter. 

Be sure to build the frames about 6” 
wider than the opening of your gar¬ 
bage-cans, so that garbage falls INTO 
the pit, rather than spills on the ground. 

Nail tightly-fitting boards (tongued- 
and-grooved, if available) across the 
top of one frame and cover with heavy 
tar-paper or roofing material. A 1” x 
4” board, about a foot long, should be 
fastened to the side opposite the hinges, 
to serve as a “handle” to hft this frame 
which will be the lid of the box. To 
prevent strain and breaking the hinges, 
as this lid will be fairly heavy, drive 
a stake in the ground behind the 
hinges. When the lid is lifted and 
t swung back, the stake will make a rest 
for the “handle”. 

At the centre of each side of the 
lower frame, nail a board about 1” x 
4” x 24” to extend down into the pit. 
Nail a 1” x 4” board joining these ex¬ 
tensions at their lower ends, to form 
a cross-bar. 


Now hinge these two frames together 
with strong 4” strap hinges. Choose 
two'2” x 4”s, long enough to reach 
well across the opening of the pit, 
place the hinged side and the 
“handle” side on the long 2” x 4”s, apd 
spike securely in place. 

Dig two 4” trenches at each side^of 
the opening of the pit, to receive the 
long 2” x 4”s, and place the whole 
framework in position over the open¬ 
ing of the pit. Lay old planks and 
boards along the long 2” x 4” supports, 
and bank them over with plenty of 
earth so that the pit will be odour- 
proof, and flies and rain will be pre¬ 
vented from entering. 

Once daily, put about one inch of 
Garbonol in a gallon can, fill with 
water, and pour down onto the cross¬ 
bar. .This bar acts as an excellent 
means of causing the disinfectant to 
spray in all directions throughout the 
pit. 

At the end of the season, remove the 
framework, scrape with a 2” board, 
scrub with an old broom soaked in 
Carbonol, and store inside for use next 
year. Fill the opening of the pit with 
earth. 

After emptying the contents of tin 
cans, 'remove the bottom of the can, 
and step on the can. This saves 
space, time, tempers, and effort in 
flattening cans. A pit of these dimen¬ 
sions will hold the refuse accumulated 
in 8 weeks by a group of 70 people. 

This type of pit has sucessfully stood 
the test of 18 summers’ satisfactory 
garbage-disposal, and has been highly 
rated and recommended by all the in¬ 
spectors of the Ontario Department of 
Health. 

GLEN ALLAN, 

Glenokawa Camp

Canadian Camping 



TENT CATERPILLARS 


The Ontario Department of Lands 
and Forests in a recent “News Release”, 
informs us that Tent Caterpillars are 
expected to be more widespread during 
1951. Egg clusters have been found 
on trees over a much wider area than 
last year. The Provincial Department 
is deeply concerned with the situation 
and is willing to cooperate with camp 
directors and other owners of forest 
land. A bulletin issued on the subject 
describes the life history of the Tent 
Caterpillar, the situation to be expect¬ 
ed in 1951, and possible means of con¬ 
trol. 

Such poisons as D.D.T. and lead 
arsenate easily kill the insect in the 
caterpillar stage. A standard stirrup 
pump with extensive hose, permits ap¬ 
plication to a greater height on trees 
and buildings. Hand operations, how¬ 
ever, have their limitations. The best- 
known means of large-scale control is 
insecticide spraying from air craft. 
“Wholesale extermination of a large 
area would be a costly undertaking”, 
the Department points out, “but co¬ 
operative control would appear feasible 
on selected summer resort areas.” 

At one camp last spring, numerous 
caterpillar tents were discovered about 
the end of May in wild cherry and 
hazel bushes around the camp property. 
Since these bushes were low, it was 
possible to bend over the branches and 
step on the “tents”, thus eliminating 
thousands in a few minutes. With the 
help of two workmen, every “tent” in 
the whole area was cleared up in this 
manner during one morning. Not 
pleasant, but very effective!—M.S.E.

FOR A COUNCIL RING FIRE 

O fire of our council ring 
Brightly burn before our eyes. 

As thy flames soar upward 
So may our thanks arise. 

Soar, O smoke of misty blue; 

Lift our gratitude on high. 

Praise be to Gitche Manitou, 

Great Spirit of the earth and sky! 

—Mary S. Edgar

sailboats and launches. Liability 
Insurance policies all contain an 
exclusion of coverage for the op¬ 
eration of automobiles, watercraft 
and aircraft. Unless this exclusion 
is deleted from your policy, you 
may be faced with the defence of 
a law suit and find your insurance 
company is not interested in your 
problems. You should check this 
point with regard to your Liability 
Insurance before opening the 1951 
season. 

(c) If you hire a contractor to do some 
construction work on your prop¬ 
erty, you may be faced with a law 
suit for personal injuries or prop¬ 
erty damage because he was work¬ 
ing for you. Does your present 
policy protect you against such 
claims? We will hazard a guess 
that 75% of you are not covered 
against loss from such a conting¬ 


ency. Check this point too! It 
can be important. 

(d) Do you serve any food, or sell any 
products which are taken off the 
premises for consumption? If so, 
is your Liability Insurance design¬ 
ed to protect you? We will again 
suggest that most of you are not 
covered against loss from this 
hazard. 

(e) Does your present policy exclude 
loss to property of others from 
fire or explosion? If it does, you 
had better get it changed because 
this can be a source of loss of large 
proportions. 

We cannot possibly cover this en¬ 
tire subject on one short article, but 
let us close this one with a word of 
advice. Buy Liability Insurance. Pur¬ 
chase adequate limits, it can be done 
for only a small additional premium. 
See that your present policy does not 
contain any exclusions which may leave 
you wide open for an uninsured loss.

In Lighter Vein 

Once there was a camper, 

She was dieting she said; 

She mustn’t eat potatoes 
Nor touch a slice of bread. 

But when it came to rich desserts, 
She could never get enough— 

Pudding, pie and doughnuts, 

Cake and creamy puff 

These, she claimed weren‘t fattening, 
Besides she liked them so. 

As we watched that camper diet, 

We beheld her waist-line grow’. 

—M.S.E. 


In the South a tornado threatened 
and the parents decided to send their 
son, Tommy, to relatives for safety. 
They wired: “Terrible tornado threat¬ 
ening. Sending Tommy”. Two days 
later they received a wire: “Returning 
Tommy. Send tornado.” 

Noah had his troubles too 

In olden times like me and you. 

For forty days he drove his ark. 

Before he found a place to park! 

Definition: A Smile—A light in the 
window of the face which shows that 
the heart is at home.
